These are teaching assumptions inspired by flash calcination, not calibrated calciner parameters. The model omits separate solid and gas phases, detailed chemistry, residence-time distributions, and industrial geometry.

The Arrhenius factor makes conversion sensitive to temperature. At 950 K the rate is 0.1 s−1^{-1}−1, a time constant of 10 s. At 900 K it falls to about 0.050 s−1^{-1}−1, and at 1000 K it rises to about 0.19 s−1^{-1}−1. Material spends about 40 s in the reactor, so a parcel that remains 50 K colder than its surroundings for part of that time leaves with noticeably more unreacted material. More heating raises the rate, but it also raises the peak temperature, which must stay below 1070 K everywhere. Because the flow speed can vary across the width, the outlet conversion is weighted by flux,

aout=1−∑ivx(yi) c(8,yi)∑ivx(yi),a_{\mathrm{out}}=1-\frac{\sum_i v_x(y_i)\,c(8,y_i)}{\sum_i v_x(y_i)},aout​=1−∑i​vx​(yi​)∑i​vx​(yi​)c(8,yi​)​,
(35)

where the sums run over the outlet cells. It must remain at least 95%95\%95%.

A finite-volume discretization with 64×3264\times3264×32 cells turns the PDE into 2×64×32=4,0962\times64\times32=4{,}0962×64×32=4,096 ordinary differential equations. Advection uses first-order upwind fluxes; diffusion uses centered fluxes with no diffusive flux through the boundaries. An explicit two-stage strong-stability-preserving Runge–Kutta method advances time in substeps of at most 0.1 s. Heater inputs are held for Δt=2\Delta t=2Δt=2 s, and integrating over one control interval defines the transition

Xk+1=F(Xk,uk),Xk∈R4096,uk∈[0,1]4,X_{k+1}=F(X_k,u_k),\qquad X_k\in\mathbb R^{4096},\quad u_k\in[0,1]^4,Xk+1​=F(Xk​,uk​),Xk​∈R4096,uk​∈[0,1]4,
(36)

which plays the role of the rollout map fk\mathbf f_kfk​ in Algorithm 1. The mesh partitions physical space; it is not a grid over the 4,096-dimensional state space. Refining it makes each rollout more expensive without changing the number of heater inputs.

Two flow profiles appear below, both with mean speed 0.2 m/s. The field-recovery problem uses a shear flow that is fastest at the center of the channel, vx(y)=0.16+0.24 η(1−η)v_x(y)=0.16+0.24\,\eta(1-\eta)vx​(y)=0.16+0.24η(1−η) m/s with η=y/2\eta=y/2η=y/2. Material then takes about 36 s to cross the reactor at the center and nearly 50 s near the walls, so a disturbance tilts and stretches as it moves. The surrogate experiment uses uniform flow at 0.2 m/s.

Restoring the operating field¶

Holding all four heaters at 0.46 for 400 s under the shear flow produces a steady operating state. Its temperature rises from about 800 K at the inlet to a maximum of 1063.54 K, and its outlet conversion is about 95.8%95.8\%95.8%. Denote its fields by T⋆T_\starT⋆​ and a⋆a_\stara⋆​. Starting from this state, a cold patch enters through the lower part of the inlet:

ΔTin(y,t)=−100exp⁡ ⁣[−(y−0.55)22(0.22)2]sin⁡2 ⁣(π(t−6)8) K,6≤t≤14 s,\Delta T_{\mathrm{in}}(y,t)=-100\exp\!\left[-\frac{(y-0.55)^2}{2(0.22)^2}\right] \sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi(t-6)}{8}\right)\ \mathrm K, \qquad 6\leq t\leq14\ \mathrm s,ΔTin​(y,t)=−100exp[−2(0.22)2(y−0.55)2​]sin2(8π(t−6)​) K,6≤t≤14 s,
(37)

and ΔTin=0\Delta T_{\mathrm{in}}=0ΔTin​=0 otherwise. Control starts at 14 s, when the whole patch has entered the reactor and is traveling through the bottom half where H1 and H2 act. If the heaters stay at 0.46, the colder material reacts too slowly: outlet conversion falls to 94.75%94.75\%94.75% and remains below the 95%95\%95% limit for 7.5 s.

The task is to return both fields to the operating state while respecting the limits. The inlet is known to have returned to its normal profile, both fields are measured exactly at each decision, and the PDE is deterministic. As in the derivation of the update, randomness enters only through the candidate controls.

Departure from the operating state is measured by the normalized field error

E(X)=12048∑cells[(T−T⋆20 K)2+(a−a⋆0.1)2].E(X)=\frac1{2048}\sum_{\text{cells}}\left[ \left(\frac{T-T_\star}{20\ \mathrm K}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{a-a_\star}{0.1}\right)^2\right].E(X)=20481​cells∑​[(20 KT−T⋆​​)2+(0.1a−a⋆​​)2].
(38)

A cell that is 20 K too cold contributes as much as a cell whose conversion is 0.1 too low. The squared error penalizes warming as well as cooling, so heat delivered to material outside the cold patch counts against a plan. Each heater acts on a quadrant of 512 cells, and four such inputs cannot set the 4,0964{,}0964,096 state values independently. Some error must remain until the cold material leaves the reactor.

MPPI plans over N=20N=20N=20 intervals, a 40 s horizon equal to the mean residence time. With u−1u_{-1}u−1​ the control applied during the previous interval, the planning objective is

J=120∑k=019[E(Xk+1)+0.014∑j=14(uk,j−0.460.05)2+0.0054∑j=14(uk,j−uk−1,j0.05)2]+E(X20).J=\frac1{20}\sum_{k=0}^{19}\left[E(X_{k+1}) +\frac{0.01}{4}\sum_{j=1}^4\left(\frac{u_{k,j}-0.46}{0.05}\right)^2 +\frac{0.005}{4}\sum_{j=1}^4\left(\frac{u_{k,j}-u_{k-1,j}}{0.05}\right)^2\right] +E(X_{20}).J=201​k=0∑19​[E(Xk+1​)+40.01​j=1∑4​(0.05uk,j​−0.46​)2+40.005​j=1∑4​(0.05uk,j​−uk−1,j​​)2]+E(X20​).
(39)

The second term discourages departures from nominal heating, and the third discourages abrupt changes between intervals. Earlier in the chapter, control effort entered only through the KL penalty and SSS contained state costs. Here JJJ plays the role of SSS and includes control terms written in physical heater units. The derivation of P⋆P^\starP⋆ used only that SSS assigns a cost to each complete candidate sequence, so these terms change the target distribution without changing the update.

The limits enter in two ways. During sampling, a candidate whose states at the 2 s decision times exceed 1070 K anywhere, or bring outlet conversion below 95%95\%95%, receives infinite cost and therefore zero weight. In the distributional objective, this restricts the reference to sequences that pass the check. That set need not be convex, so the mean of the resulting Gibbs distribution need not satisfy the limits, as in Exercise Exercise 4. Each proposed update therefore requires its own check before it can replace the stored plan.

Sampling in a bounded control space¶

A plan contains 20×4=8020\times4=8020×4=80 heater values. Sampling each independently would produce irregular schedules and spend samples on rapid fluctuations that the third term of JJJ penalizes. As in the aircraft example, a candidate is described by a few smooth parameters: six knots for each heater, linearly interpolated to the 20 decision times. This gives 24 sampled parameters, collected in a 6×46\times46×4 array zzz.

Heater inputs must stay in [0,1][0,1][0,1], while Gaussian samples are unbounded. Clipping would change the distribution of the clipped values, as noted after Algorithm 1. Instead, a logistic map takes latent parameters to physical knot values,

uknots(z)=sigmoid⁡(logit⁡(useed)+0.12 z),u_{\mathrm{knots}}(z)=\operatorname{sigmoid}\bigl(\operatorname{logit}(u_{\mathrm{seed}})+0.12\,z\bigr),uknots​(z)=sigmoid(logit(useed​)+0.12z),
(40)

applied elementwise. The array useedu_{\mathrm{seed}}useed​ contains the stored plan evaluated at the six knot times, so z=0z=0z=0 reproduces the stored plan up to interpolation error. The derivative of the sigmoid is u(1−u)u(1-u)u(1−u), which is about 0.25 near u=0.46u=0.46u=0.46. A latent change of 0.7, one standard deviation of the sampling distribution below, therefore moves a knot by about 0.12×0.7×0.25≈0.0210.12\times0.7\times0.25\approx0.0210.12×0.7×0.25≈0.021, or two percentage points of heating.

Gaussian densities are defined on zzz. The reference is p0=N(0,0.49I)p_0=\mathcal N(0,0.49I)p0​=N(0,0.49I) and the proposal is qμ=N(μ,0.49I)q_\mu=\mathcal N(\mu,0.49I)qμ​=N(μ,0.49I). At each decision the decoder and the reference stay fixed while μ\muμ starts at zero. Each of four updates draws K=256K=256K=256 candidates z(i)∼qμz^{(i)}\sim q_\muz(i)∼qμ​, decodes them, simulates them in the PDE, and computes

wi∝exp⁡ ⁣[−J(z(i))λ]p0(z(i))qμ(z(i)),μweighted=∑i=1Kwi z(i),λ=0.01.w_i\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac{J(z^{(i)})}{\lambda}\right] \frac{p_0(z^{(i)})}{q_\mu(z^{(i)})}, \qquad \mu_{\mathrm{weighted}}=\sum_{i=1}^Kw_i\,z^{(i)}, \qquad \lambda=0.01.wi​∝exp[−λJ(z(i))​]qμ​(z(i))p0​(z(i))​,μweighted​=i=1∑K​wi​z(i),λ=0.01.
(41)

This is the importance-corrected update in latent coordinates, with Σ=0.49I\Sigma=0.49IΣ=0.49I and the mean μ\muμ in place of the nominal controls. The weighting temperature λ\lambdaλ is dimensionless, like JJJ, and unrelated to temperature in kelvin. Since latent zero decodes to the stored plan, the KL penalty charges for changing that plan, not for heating as such. This is the alternative, noted with the reference distribution, of centering the reference on a baseline sequence, with the previous plan as the baseline. The average is taken in latent coordinates, so the decoded heater schedule generally differs from the weighted average of the candidates’ physical schedules.

The temperature sets which cost differences matter. At the first decision, the stored plan has J=0.0488J=0.0488J=0.0488. Before correction, a candidate whose cost exceeds another’s by λlog⁡2≈0.0069\lambda\log2\approx0.0069λlog2≈0.0069, about 14%14\%14% of that value, receives half the weight.

The likelihood correction changes the weights substantially once μ\muμ has moved. At the fourth update of the first decision, after three accepted updates, candidate 12 had cost 0.05649 and candidate 180 had cost 0.05840. Exponential cost weighting alone would give candidate 12 about e0.191≈1.21e^{0.191}\approx1.21e0.191≈1.21 times the weight of candidate 180. Its recorded weight, 0.0682, was instead less than half of candidate 180’s weight, 0.1565. The ratio corresponds to corrected costs that differ by −λlog⁡(0.0682/0.1565)≈0.0083-\lambda\log(0.0682/0.1565)\approx0.0083−λlog(0.0682/0.1565)≈0.0083 in favor of candidate 180, so the correction term contributes about 0.0102. Candidate 12 lies farther in the direction in which the proposal had already moved, where the proposal samples more often than the reference. Exercise Exercise 6 works through this calculation.

Validating and executing a sampled update¶

Each update ends by checking the proposed mean. The controller decodes μ+α(μweighted−μ)\mu+\alpha(\mu_{\mathrm{weighted}}-\mu)μ+α(μweighted​−μ) for step fractions α∈{1,12,14,18}\alpha\in\{1,\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac18\}α∈{1,21​,41​,81​} in turn, and accepts the first that lowers JJJ below the stored plan’s value and passes a finer check. The finer check records the PDE state every 0.25 s over the 40 s plan, followed by another 40 s at nominal heating, and tests both limits at every record. If no step fraction succeeds, both μ\muμ and the stored plan remain unchanged.

After four updates, the controller applies the first 2 s of the stored plan to the PDE, shifts the plan by one interval, and appends nominal heating. The stored plan is the exact heater sequence that passed validation; its six-knot approximation useedu_{\mathrm{seed}}useed​ only centers the next round of sampling. Because the plant is the same deterministic PDE with a known inlet, executing the first action reproduces the predicted state. The shifted plan followed by nominal heating then repeats a trajectory that has already passed the finer check, except for its final 2 s. The validation tail at nominal heating is what makes this continuation available: if every later update is rejected, the controller still holds a checked plan. Receding-horizon control develops this property, recursive feasibility, with terminal conditions in place of a simulated tail.

The procedure needs a feasible plan at the first decision. Unchanged heating does not qualify, since it violates the conversion limit. The experiment supplies an initial schedule that holds H1 at 0.50 for 8 s and returns it to 0.46 over the following 8 s, with the other heaters at nominal. This schedule is given to the controller, not found by it; MPPI starts from it and revises it at every decision.

Recorded recovery¶

All three schedules start from the same disturbed state at 14 s and are recorded until 80 s on a 0.25 s output grid. The integrated field error is ∫1480E(X(t)) dt\int_{14}^{80}E(X(t))\,dt∫1480​E(X(t))dt, and heating energy is the integral of the mean heater fraction over the same interval. Both are measured in seconds; heating energy counts seconds at full average heating, since the model has no heat capacity to convert it to joules.

ScheduleIntegrated field errorHeating energyMaximum temperatureLowest outlet conversion
Unchanged heating3.709 s30.360 s1063.54 K94.747%94.747\%94.747%
Supplied initial schedule, executed unchanged2.098 s30.484 s1066.94 K95.271%95.271\%95.271%
MPPI1.962 s30.439 s1066.16 K95.329%95.329\%95.329%

The supplied schedule alone removes 43%43\%43% of the integrated error of unchanged heating and restores the conversion limit. MPPI removes 47.1%47.1\%47.1%, which is 6.5%6.5\%6.5% less error than the supplied schedule, while using slightly less heat than that schedule and staying 3.8 K below the temperature limit.

The controls in Figure 8 follow the patch. MPPI raises H1 by about five percentage points while the patch crosses the upstream bottom quadrant, then returns it to nominal by about 32 s. Between about 36 and 62 s it lowers H2, by up to 0.8 percentage points near 48 s, as material warmed by H1 passes through the downstream bottom quadrant; the squared error penalizes that excess warmth. The top heaters change by less than one percentage point. Outlet conversion still dips as the patch leaves, but its lowest value is 95.33%95.33\%95.33% instead of 94.75%94.75\%94.75%.

The sampling statistics show how much of this result comes from accepted updates. Over 33 decisions, 24 of 132 updates were accepted. Only four of the accepted updates used the full weighted mean; the other 20 needed a step fraction of 12\tfrac1221​ or less. Nine acceptances occurred in the first three decisions and eleven more between 32 and 42 s, as the patch approached the outlet. From 44 s on, only 3 of 72 updates were accepted. By then the stored plan was already returning to nominal heating, and random perturbations tended to add error to a field that was recovering on its own. The effective sample size ranged from 19.8 to 64.1 of 256 candidates, and between 108 and 217 candidates per batch passed the constraint check. With the weight concentrated on a few dozen candidates, the weighted mean is a noisy proposal, and the step fractions trade progress for reliability.

The opening decision was also repeated with three optimizer seeds at each of 128, 256, and 512 candidates. All nine runs lowered the objective of the supplied schedule, by between 5.3%5.3\%5.3% and 6.7%6.7\%6.7%. The effective sample size grew with the number of candidates, from 4.3–18.9 at 128 to 32.5–63.0 at 512. The final objectives did not improve with the count: their spread across seeds at a fixed count exceeded the differences between the averages at different counts. These repetitions measure optimizer variability at one physical state. They do not establish that the recorded plan is globally optimal.

Planning took 13.9 s per decision on average, including the finer checks and first-use compilation. This is longer than the 2 s control interval: the recording is an offline computation, not a demonstration of real-time control. The numerical model was checked separately by repeating the executed MPPI controls with halved integration steps, which changes the temperature field by 0.0014 K root-mean-square, and on a 128×64128\times64128×64 mesh, which changes it by 0.78 K. The finer mesh reaches 1068.42 K and a lowest outlet conversion of 95.36%95.36\%95.36%, still within both limits. First-order upwind advection adds numerical diffusion of roughly vxΔx/2≈0.013v_x\Delta x/2\approx0.013vx​Δx/2≈0.013 m2^22/s, much larger than DDD, so part of the visible spreading of the patch is a property of the discretization.

Planning with a learned surrogate¶

Each recovery decision simulated 256 candidates over 20 intervals in each of four updates, or 20,48020{,}48020,480 interval rollouts before validation. For this coarse PDE the budget is affordable. A finer mesh, separate gas and solid phases, or a computational fluid dynamics model of an industrial calciner would make it expensive. A common response is to learn a fast approximate transition model, a surrogate, from simulations and to use it for the candidate rollouts. MPPI requires only rollouts and costs, so the substitution changes no part of the update. It changes which model ranks the candidates: the weights now favor candidates that the surrogate predicts to be good.

The surrogate experiment uses the uniform-flow version of the reactor with a different task. Nominal heating is 0.48 in all four quadrants, and the inlet temperature 800+10cos⁡(πy/2)+gt800+10\cos(\pi y/2)+g_t800+10cos(πy/2)+gt​ K fluctuates. The deviation gtg_tgt​ follows the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model of the aircraft example with correlation time 20 s and stationary standard deviation 15 K, held constant over each 2 s interval and observed at each decision. The objective is economic: use as little heat as possible while keeping outlet conversion at least 95%95\%95% and temperature at most 1070 K. The planning cost averages, over 20 steps,

ℓk=14∑j=14uk,j+5[(0.95−aout,k+1)+0.05]2+10[(max⁡Tk+1−1070 K)+20 K]2+0.054∑j=14(uk,j−uk−1,j0.1)2,\ell_k=\frac14\sum_{j=1}^4u_{k,j} +5\left[\frac{(0.95-a_{\mathrm{out},k+1})_+}{0.05}\right]^2 +10\left[\frac{(\max T_{k+1}-1070\ \mathrm K)_+}{20\ \mathrm K}\right]^2 +\frac{0.05}{4}\sum_{j=1}^4\left(\frac{u_{k,j}-u_{k-1,j}}{0.1}\right)^2,ℓk​=41​j=1∑4​uk,j​+5[0.05(0.95−aout,k+1​)+​​]2+10[20 K(maxTk+1​−1070 K)+​​]2+40.05​j=1∑4​(0.1uk,j​−uk−1,j​​)2,
(42)

where (⋅)+=max⁡(⋅,0)(\cdot)_+=\max(\cdot,0)(⋅)+​=max(⋅,0) and the conversion and temperature are evaluated at the end of interval kkk.

The surrogate is a residual convolutional network that predicts the change of both fields over one 2 s interval. Its six input channels are the normalized temperature and reactant fields, the map of heater fractions, the normalized inlet temperature, and two coordinate channels. Four 3×33\times33×3 convolutions with 16 hidden channels and dilations 1,2,4,11,2,4,11,2,4,1 let each output cell depend on inputs up to eight cells away, more than the 3.2 cells that material travels in one interval. After each predicted step, the reactant fraction is projected onto [0,1][0,1][0,1]; temperature is not modified. Training used 256 PDE episodes of 120 s with varied heating, warm and cold starts, smooth spatial transients, and inlet fluctuations, split by whole episode into 179 training, 38 validation, and 39 test episodes. The loss combined one-step error, five-step rollout error, and outlet error. The checkpoint used here was selected after three epochs of Adam within a local CPU budget.

Held-out 40 s rollouts, 39 test episodesResult
Temperature root-mean-square error4.59 K
Outlet-conversion mean absolute error0.0039
95th percentile of peak-temperature underprediction8.31 K
Largest reactant-fraction bound excess before projection0.068

These averages must be read against the margins that decide feasibility. Under constant heating, the lowest outlet conversion in the trials below is 95.09%95.09\%95.09%, a margin of 0.09 percentage points, while the surrogate’s average conversion error is 0.39 percentage points. A plan accepted on the surrogate’s predictions alone could violate the conversion limit in the PDE, and an 8 K underprediction of the peak temperature could hide a violation of the temperature limit.

The controller therefore keeps two roles for the PDE. Every applied control advances the PDE under the realized inlet, and every proposed plan is simulated in the PDE before it is accepted. The planner samples K=128K=128K=128 candidates in latent coordinates with u(z)=sigmoid⁡(logit⁡(0.48)+0.35z)u(z)=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\operatorname{logit}(0.48)+0.35z)u(z)=sigmoid(logit(0.48)+0.35z) and the reference p0=N(0,0.49I)p_0=\mathcal N(0,0.49I)p0​=N(0,0.49I), which now decodes to constant nominal heating. Its KL penalty charges departures from nominal heating, while the proposal mean is initialized from the shifted previous plan. Candidate costs come from surrogate rollouts, and the weights use λ=0.025\lambda=0.025λ=0.025. A candidate that uses one percentage point less heat on average, with no penalty active, receives about e0.01/0.025≈1.5e^{0.01/0.025}\approx1.5e0.01/0.025≈1.5 times the weight. After each of two updates per decision, the weighted mean is accepted only if it lowers the surrogate cost and a PDE rollout under the conditional mean inlet keeps conversion at or above 95%95\%95% and temperature at or below 1070 K at every 2 s output. Otherwise the previous plan is kept. If the shifted previous plan fails the PDE check at the next decision, constant nominal heating is checked instead; if both fail, the episode stops and records a planning failure.

Two forecast variants separate reaction to the observed inlet from planning under its uncertainty, as in the aircraft example. The mean-forecast controller scores each candidate under the conditional mean of the future inlet. The stochastic controller scores it under four conditional futures, shared by all candidates, and averages the four costs before weighting.

Surrogate and PDE planning compared¶

Eight paired trials start from the warm state and last 160 s. Within a trial, constant heating and both MPPI controllers face the same realized inlet sequence.

ControllerMean heating energyLowest outlet conversionHighest temperatureAccepted updatesPlanning time per decision
Constant heating76.800 s95.09%95.09\%95.09%1059.5 Knonenone
Surrogate MPPI, mean forecast75.807 s95.30%95.30\%95.30%1051.9 K127 of 12801.32 s
Surrogate MPPI, stochastic forecast75.759 s95.16%95.16\%95.16%1052.4 K143 of 12804.45 s

Lowest and highest values are taken over all trials at the 2 s outputs. No episode stopped, and every execution stayed within both limits on the 2 s grid and on a separate 0.1 s audit of the executed controls. Paired differences in heating energy, with 95%95\%95% Student-t intervals over the eight trials, are −0.99±0.30-0.99\pm0.30−0.99±0.30 s for mean-forecast MPPI minus constant heating, −1.04±0.34-1.04\pm0.34−1.04±0.34 s for stochastic MPPI minus constant heating, and −0.048±0.099-0.048\pm0.099−0.048±0.099 s for stochastic minus mean-forecast MPPI. Both MPPI variants use about 1.3%1.3\%1.3% less heat than constant heating. The trials do not establish a difference between the two forecast variants. About one proposed update in ten was accepted.

To isolate the effect of the rollout model, the same planner was run from the warm state with zero inlet deviation, once with surrogate rollouts and once with PDE rollouts, using the same random seed and settings. Each resulting 40 s plan was then evaluated in the PDE on 32 fresh inlet futures. The first heater commands were nearly identical, (0.484,0.474,0.486,0.480)(0.484,0.474,0.486,0.480)(0.484,0.474,0.486,0.480) from the surrogate and (0.484,0.472,0.486,0.478)(0.484,0.472,0.486,0.478)(0.484,0.472,0.486,0.478) from the PDE, and the held-out PDE costs were 0.47331 and 0.47250. Planning took 14.57 s with the surrogate and 11.25 s with the PDE, both including PDE validation and the recording of candidate snapshots. For this coarse PDE the surrogate brought no speed advantage. A surrogate pays for itself only when the model it replaces is substantially more expensive to roll out.

The two plans nearly coincide because of the structure of ℓk\ell_kℓk​. For a candidate that triggers neither penalty, the cost consists of mean heating and the slew term, which depend only on the controls. The surrogate and the PDE assign such a candidate the same cost. For both selected plans, the cost on the planning forecasts agreed with the held-out PDE cost to within 10-6. Such agreement between different models and inlet futures means that the penalties contributed essentially nothing in either evaluation. The rollout model affects the weights only through the penalties, that is, through deciding which low-heating candidates violate the conversion limit and which high-heating candidates exceed the temperature limit. Surrogate accuracy matters near the boundary of the feasible set, which is also where an economic objective drives the plan. Average errors over held-out trajectories do not measure accuracy there. The PDE acceptance check instead tests the one plan that will be executed, under the conditional mean inlet.

Both experiments use the same structure. Sampling explores a small, bounded parameterization of the heater schedule; exponential weights with a likelihood correction propose an update; and the full model decides whether the update replaces a plan that is already known to be feasible. In the recovery experiment the full model also generates the candidate costs. In the surrogate experiment a learned model generates them, and its errors matter where the constraints are nearly active.

Summary and Outlook¶

MPPI begins with the single-shooting rollout and changes how its candidate inputs are combined. A reference distribution favors small inputs; exponential state-cost weights favor useful trajectories; a Gaussian fit turns the resulting distribution into a stored control sequence. Importance correction preserves the target when samples are drawn around a nonzero nominal sequence.

The aircraft application separates control exploration from wind uncertainty and averages wind costs before assigning a candidate its weight. Increasing the number of candidate controls and increasing the number of wind futures address different estimation errors. Neither guarantees that a weighted mean is feasible or improves the cost, so candidate updates are validated before they replace the stored plan.

The reactor application uses the same update on a discretized PDE with 4,096 state values. Six bounded knots per heater reduce the search to 24 latent parameters, in which the Gaussian densities and the likelihood correction are computed, and candidates that violate a limit receive zero weight. Because the mean of feasible candidates need not be feasible, each proposed update is checked in the PDE, damped when necessary, and otherwise rejected; once the field was recovering, most updates were rejected. Replacing the PDE by a learned surrogate in the sampling loop changes the model that ranks candidates, while the PDE still decides which plan is executed. With an economic objective, the surrogate’s errors matter mainly near the operating limits, which is where the plan operates.

The controller still needs an execution rule. Applying one action, observing the result, and solving again provides feedback even though each stored sequence is open loop. Receding-horizon control develops that rule further, including the choice of horizon, terminal conditions, and feasibility safeguards. These questions apply whether the planner uses derivatives or sampled trajectories.

The method’s name also reflects a connection to expectations over entire stochastic paths. Path-integral stochastic control, after stochastic dynamic programming, develops that connection and states the additional assumptions under which path weighting yields an optimal current feedback action.

Computational Sources¶

The aircraft and reactor experiments use small numerical modules and read precomputed results when the book is built. The aircraft evaluator averages each candidate’s costs over a shared ensemble of possible wind futures.

  • Gaussian importance weights and mean updates

  • Aircraft model, wind scenarios, and trajectory optimizer

  • Aircraft experiment and figure generator

  • ERA5 numerical snapshot and provenance and checksums

  • Reactor PDE, heaters, and inlet disturbances and shear flow and cold inlet pulse

  • Direct-PDE field recovery

  • Convolutional surrogate and surrogate MPPI with PDE acceptance checks

  • Reactor experiment stages

  • Recovery decisions and surrogate trials

The experiment scripts record the physical parameters, planner settings, seeds, and validation diagnostics alongside their results. The aircraft replay and the reactor replay display recorded simulations without a Python kernel. Regeneration commands are in the repository README.

Exercises¶

Exercise 1 (Weights and control updates)

An MPPI iteration has scalar nominal control u=0u=0u=0, perturbations (−1,0,1)(-1,0,1)(−1,0,1), corrected trajectory costs (log⁡4,log⁡2,0)(\log4,\log2,0)(log4,log2,0), and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1.

(a) Compute the normalized weights and the updated control.

(b) Add 1000 to every cost. Explain why the mathematical update is unchanged and how to compute it without numerical underflow.

(c) Keep the corrected costs fixed and let λ\lambdaλ approach zero. Which perturbation determines the limiting update?

Solution to Exercise 1

(a) The unnormalized weights are (1/4,1/2,1)(1/4,1/2,1)(1/4,1/2,1), whose sum is 7/47/47/4. The normalized weights are (1/7,2/7,4/7)(1/7,2/7,4/7)(1/7,2/7,4/7), giving u+=−(1/7)+(4/7)=3/7u^+=-(1/7)+(4/7)=3/7u+=−(1/7)+(4/7)=3/7.

(b) The common factor e−1000e^{-1000}e−1000 cancels between numerator and denominator. Direct evaluation would underflow in ordinary floating-point arithmetic. Subtracting the minimum corrected cost before exponentiating recovers the original three weights.

(c) The unique minimum cost belongs to perturbation 1. Its normalized weight approaches one, so u+→1u^+\to1u+→1. The qualification that corrected costs are fixed matters: a likelihood correction can itself depend on λ\lambdaλ.

Exercise 2 (The likelihood correction)

Consider the deterministic rollout xk+1=xk+hvkx_{k+1}=x_k+hv_kxk+1​=xk​+hvk​ with x0=0x_0=0x0​=0, target a=1a=1a=1, N=10N=10N=10 intervals of length h=0.1h=0.1h=0.1, and terminal cost κ2(xN−a)2\tfrac\kappa2(x_N-a)^22κ​(xN​−a)2 with κ=4\kappa=4κ=4. Set λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5 and choose a Gaussian reference covariance Σh=λ/(rh)\Sigma_h=\lambda/(rh)Σh​=λ/(rh) with r=1r=1r=1, so its KL penalty gives the quadratic mean-control effort. The proposal mean is uk=0.4u_k=0.4uk​=0.4 at every step.

(a) Complete the square in the Gibbs density to find its mean. You may use the fact that the mean of a Gaussian equals the minimizer of the quadratic in its negative log density.

(b) Find the mean estimated when the weights include the state cost but omit the reference-to-proposal density ratio.

(c) Implement both estimators and compare their mean control, averaged over the ten time slots, as the sample count increases. Does increasing the sample count correct the discrepancy in part (b)?

Solution to Exercise 2

(a) Up to a constant, the negative log Gibbs density is

rh2λ∑kvk2+κ2λ(h∑kvk−a)2.\frac{rh}{2\lambda}\sum_kv_k^2 +\frac\kappa{2\lambda}\left(h\sum_kv_k-a\right)^2.2λrh​k∑​vk2​+2λκ​(hk∑​vk​−a)2.
(43)

Its first-order condition is rvk+κ(h∑jvj−a)=0r v_k+\kappa(h\sum_jv_j-a)=0rvk​+κ(h∑j​vj​−a)=0. All coordinates of its minimizer are equal, giving

EP⋆vk=κar+κNh=0.8.\mathbb E_{P^\star}v_k=\frac{\kappa a}{r+\kappa Nh}=0.8.EP⋆​vk​=r+κNhκa​=0.8.
(44)

The result is independent of the proposal mean because the likelihood ratio cancels the proposal density in the expectation.

(b) Omitting that ratio replaces the reference quadratic ∑kvk2\sum_kv_k^2∑k​vk2​ by ∑k(vk−0.4)2\sum_k(v_k-0.4)^2∑k​(vk​−0.4)2. The corresponding first-order condition is r(vk−0.4)+κ(h∑jvj−a)=0r(v_k-0.4)+\kappa(h\sum_jv_j-a)=0r(vk​−0.4)+κ(h∑j​vj​−a)=0, so its mean is

0.4r+κar+κNh=0.88.\frac{0.4r+\kappa a}{r+\kappa Nh}=0.88.r+κNh0.4r+κa​=0.88.
(45)

Thus the two procedures converge to different expectations.

(c) A minimal implementation uses the same perturbations for both estimates so that their difference is easier to observe:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(728)
N, h, r, kappa, lam = 10, 0.1, 1.0, 4.0, 0.5
U = np.full(N, 0.4)
for K in (1_000, 10_000, 100_000):
    eps = rng.normal(size=(K, N)) * np.sqrt(lam / (r * h))
    inputs = U + eps
    cost = 0.5 * kappa * (h * inputs.sum(axis=1) - 1.0) ** 2
    corrected = cost + h * r * (eps @ U)
    estimates = []
    for scores in (corrected, cost):
        weights = np.exp(-(scores - scores.min()) / lam)
        weights /= weights.sum()
        estimates.append((weights @ inputs).mean())
    print(K, *estimates)

The estimates approach 0.8 and 0.88. More samples reduce Monte Carlo error; they do not repair an omitted likelihood ratio. Individual runs need not approach their limits monotonically.

Exercise 3 (Stochastic aircraft rollouts and expected cost)

An aircraft simulator accepts a control sequence U\mathbf UU and a gust history WWW, and returns cost C(U,W)C(\mathbf U,W)C(U,W). The objective is EWC(U,W)\mathbb E_W C(\mathbf U,W)EW​C(U,W).

(a) A sampling optimizer generates one gust history per candidate control sequence and assigns weight proportional to e−C(U,W)/λe^{-C(\mathbf U,W)/\lambda}e−C(U,W)/λ. Explain why collecting more such weighted samples does not generally recover the intended expected-cost objective.

(b) Consider a safe candidate with constant cost 1 and a risky candidate with cost 0 with probability 0.9 and 20 with probability 0.1. At λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, compare their expected costs and their exponential scores −log⁡E[e−C]-\log\mathbb E[e^{-C}]−logE[e−C].

(c) Describe a sampling design that ranks candidate controls by an estimate of expected cost. Does this design guarantee that the weighted mean is optimal or feasible?

Solution to Exercise 3

(a) For a fixed candidate, averaging the weights estimates EW[e−C/λ]\mathbb E_W[e^{-C/\lambda}]EW​[e−C/λ], whereas the desired score depends on EWC\mathbb E_W CEW​C. The exponential is nonlinear. Favorable gust histories receive disproportionate weight, so this procedure can favor a candidate whose expected cost is larger. The reference-to-proposal correction for control sampling does not remove this difference in the disturbance objective.

(b) The safe candidate has expected cost 1 and exponential score 1. The risky candidate has expected cost 2 but exponential score −log⁡(0.9+0.1e−20)≈0.105-\log(0.9+0.1e^{-20})\approx0.105−log(0.9+0.1e−20)≈0.105. Expected cost favors the safe candidate; the exponential score favors the risky candidate.

(c) For each candidate, simulate multiple gust histories and form C^(U)=L−1∑ℓ=1LC(U,W(ℓ))\widehat C(\mathbf U)=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L C(\mathbf U,W^{(\ell)})C(U)=L−1∑ℓ=1L​C(U,W(ℓ)). Then use C^\widehat CC as the candidate score in the sampling optimizer. Shared gust histories across candidates can make paired comparisons less variable. As the number of disturbance samples increases, this score estimates the intended expected cost. The subsequent Gaussian mean fit need not minimize that cost over deterministic plans. Finite sampling introduces further error, and an average of feasible plans may violate nonconvex constraints. The proposed plan still needs cost and feasibility checks.

Exercise 4 (Shifting a plan and checking its mean)

A controller stores (u0,u1,u2)=(0.6,0.4,0.2)(u_0,u_1,u_2)=(0.6,0.4,0.2)(u0​,u1​,u2​)=(0.6,0.4,0.2) for three intervals. After the first interval it observes a new state.

(a) Which control was executed, and what sequence initializes the next planning problem if the final control is repeated? What other input to the rollout changes at this observation?

(b) Consider the separate one-step system x1=ux_1=ux1​=u with terminal constraint x1∈[−1.1,−0.9]∪[0.9,1.1]x_1\in[-1.1,-0.9]\cup[0.9,1.1]x1​∈[−1.1,−0.9]∪[0.9,1.1]. Two feasible candidates are u=−1u=-1u=−1 and u=1u=1u=1. Is their equally weighted mean feasible? What should an implementation with a validated incumbent do if this mean is proposed?

Solution to Exercise 4

(a) The controller executed 0.6. Its shifted initial guess is (0.4,0.2,0.2)(0.4,0.2,0.2)(0.4,0.2,0.2), and the measured state becomes the initial state for every new rollout. The guess is then updated by sampling; it is not a commitment to execute all three entries.

(b) The mean is u=0u=0u=0, which produces x1=0x_1=0x1​=0 outside both allowed intervals. Feasible samples do not ensure a feasible mean under nonconvex constraints. The implementation should validate the proposal and retain the feasible incumbent when that validation fails, as in the aircraft example.

Exercise 5 (The computational budget of a reactor decision)

The field-recovery controller of the reactor example draws K=256K=256K=256 latent arrays in each of four updates per decision. Each candidate is simulated for 20 intervals of 2 s, with PDE substeps of at most 0.1 s.

(a) How many state values does a candidate rollout advance at each substep, and how many numbers does the weighted mean average?

(b) Ignoring validation, how many 2 s interval simulations and at least how many substeps does one decision require?

(c) The mesh is refined from 64×3264\times3264×32 to 128×64128\times64128×64 cells. Using the advective condition vxΔt≤Δxv_x\Delta t\leq\Delta xvx​Δt≤Δx with vx≤0.22v_x\leq0.22vx​≤0.22 m/s, check that the 0.1 s substep cap still determines the substep size. By what factor do the state dimension, the number of sampled parameters, and the work per decision change?

(d) The six-knot parameterization cannot represent every sequence of 80 heater values. Give an example of a schedule it excludes, and explain what this restriction implies for the claim that the recorded MPPI schedule is optimal.

Solution to Exercise 5

(a) Each of the 2,0482{,}0482,048 cells carries a temperature and a reactant fraction, so a rollout advances 4,0964{,}0964,096 state values. The weighted mean averages the 6×4=246\times4=246×4=24 latent parameters.

(b) One decision simulates 256×4×20=20,480256\times4\times20=20{,}480256×4×20=20,480 intervals. Each interval needs at least 2/0.1=202/0.1=202/0.1=20 substeps, so at least 409,600409{,}600409,600 substeps are required, each evaluating the right-hand side twice in the two-stage Runge–Kutta method.

(c) The refined mesh has Δx=8/128=0.0625\Delta x=8/128=0.0625Δx=8/128=0.0625 m, so the advective condition allows Δt≤0.0625/0.22≈0.28\Delta t\leq0.0625/0.22\approx0.28Δt≤0.0625/0.22≈0.28 s, and the 0.1 s cap remains binding. The state dimension grows by a factor of four, to 16,38416{,}38416,384. The number of sampled parameters stays 24. Each substep updates four times as many cells, so the work per decision grows by about a factor of four. The weights and the update keep the same dimension.

(d) A single 2 s increase of one heater in the middle of the horizon, with all neighboring values at nominal, is not piecewise linear between the six knot times and cannot be represented. MPPI searches only within the knot family, so the recorded schedule is at best a good member of that family. Finite sampling, the Gaussian mean fit, the regularizing reference, and the step fractions limit even that statement, so the result supports an improvement over the supplied schedule, not optimality.

Every sample beyond a bound then produces the same control and the same cost. Exercise 7 (When the rollout model matters)

In the surrogate experiment, each step of a candidate’s planning cost is ℓk\ell_kℓk​, combining mean heating, a conversion penalty, a temperature penalty, and a slew penalty.

(a) Suppose that, for some candidate, neither penalty is active under the surrogate or under the PDE. Show that both models assign it the same planning cost. Which candidates can the surrogate’s errors affect?

(b) The surrogate’s 95th-percentile peak-temperature underprediction on held-out rollouts is 8.31 K. A proposed plan has a predicted maximum temperature of 1064 K. Does this establish that it satisfies the 1070 K limit in the PDE? Which step of the controller protects the plant, and under which inlet sequence does that step check the plan?

(c) An alternative tightens the limits used inside surrogate rollouts to 1070−δ1070-\delta1070−δ K and 95%+ε95\%+\varepsilon95%+ε. Describe the tradeoff in choosing δ\deltaδ and ε\varepsilonε when the objective is to minimize heating.

(d) At one state, planning with the surrogate took 14.57 s and planning with the PDE took 11.25 s. When would you expect a surrogate to reduce planning time? What evidence would you require before removing the PDE acceptance check?

Solution to Exercise 7

(a) Without active penalties, ℓk\ell_kℓk​ reduces to mean heating plus the slew term, both functions of the controls alone. Any rollouts that remain valid therefore give the same cost under either model. Surrogate errors can change the cost only of candidates for which at least one model predicts an active penalty, that is, candidates near the conversion or temperature limit. Minimizing heating pushes the plan toward the conversion limit, so these are the candidates that matter.

(b) No. The 8.31 K figure is a percentile over held-out windows, not a bound: one window in twenty underpredicted by more, and an optimized plan is not drawn from the held-out distribution. Adding 8.31 K to 1064 K already exceeds 1070 K. The PDE acceptance check simulates the proposed plan before it replaces the stored one. It uses the conditional mean of the future inlet, so it does not guarantee feasibility under the inlet that is actually realized. The audit on a 0.1 s grid checks the executed controls only after the fact.

(c) Larger margins make surrogate rollouts reject more candidates near the limits. Fewer proposals then fail the PDE check, and violations under the realized inlet become less likely, but the controller gives up heating reductions that were feasible. Smaller margins allow plans closer to the limits, at the price of more rejected proposals and less protection against surrogate error and inlet uncertainty. Margins calibrated from surrogate errors near the limits, rather than from average errors, would make this choice less arbitrary.

(d) A surrogate reduces planning time when rollouts of the full model dominate the computation and the surrogate is much cheaper to evaluate in large batches, for example with a finer mesh, multiphase physics, or computational fluid dynamics. Removing the PDE check would require evidence about errors near the constraint boundary for the kinds of plans the optimizer proposes, not only average errors on training-like trajectories, together with closed-loop trials whose executed controls are audited in the full model.

Exercise 8 (A surrogate for field recovery)

The field-recovery experiment plans with the PDE, while the available surrogate was trained for the uniform-flow reactor with random inlet fluctuations. This project closes that gap using the modules listed under Computational Sources.

(a) Generate PDE training episodes under the shear flow that include cold inlet pulses with varied position, width, depth, and duration, together with varied heating schedules. Train the residual network and report held-out errors for the field error EEE, the peak temperature, and the outlet conversion.

(b) Replace PDE rollouts by surrogate rollouts when scoring candidates in the recovery controller, keeping the PDE validation unchanged. Compare integrated field error, accepted updates, and planning time with the direct-PDE recording.

(c) Test the controller on a pulse whose position lies outside the training range. Which recorded diagnostics would show that the surrogate is unreliable before a plan is executed?

Solution to Exercise 8

Answers depend on the training data and budget. Useful comparisons keep the initial state, supplied schedule, planner settings, and optimizer seeds fixed, so that differences come from the rollout model. Since the tracking objective depends on the entire field, surrogate errors affect every candidate’s cost, unlike in the economic objective of Exercise Exercise 7. When the surrogate ranks candidates differently from the PDE, an accepted update can lower the surrogate objective while raising the PDE objective, so both should be recorded for every proposal. For part (c), the fraction of proposals rejected by the PDE check, the gap between the surrogate’s predicted objective and the PDE objective of each proposal, and raw reactant-fraction values outside [0,1][0,1][0,1] before projection all signal that the surrogate is operating outside its training distribution.

Self-checks¶

Exercise 9 (Sampling and feedback)

What makes the executed controller a feedback controller: drawing many trajectories, or conditioning a new plan on the next observed state?

Solution to Exercise 9

Conditioning a new plan on the observed state supplies feedback. A control sequence computed from many samples and then frozen still executes open loop.

Exercise 10 (Randomness in the reactor recovery)

In the field-recovery experiment, which quantities are random: the plant, the inlet, or the candidate controls? What changes when the optimizer seed changes?

Solution to Exercise 10

Only the candidate controls are random. The PDE is deterministic and the inlet is known after the pulse, so random numbers serve only to explore heater schedules. A different seed changes the sampled candidates and therefore the plan. Across the nine repetitions of the opening decision, the final objective varied by about 1.5%1.5\%1.5%.
